summary: Describes a vendor extension to the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, extending its test protocol so it can measure capacity metrics such as available path capacity, tight section capacity, and UDP delivery rate in forward and reverse directions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds extra measurements to a tool that checks the network, such as how much traffic a path can carry, in each direction.

subtitle: Extensions to TWAMP for measuring network path capacity in both directions.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to measure path capacity (how much traffic a link can handle) and UDP delivery rate in both directions, but TWAMP only measures round-trip behavior and does not natively support capacity testing.
tldr.mechanism: The Ericsson TWAMP Value-Added Octets feature adds 10 octets to test packets containing version, flags, the last sequence number in a packet train, and a desired reverse packet interval, allowing the reflector to identify and send back trains at specified rates.
tldr.outcome: A TWAMP reflector can now measure capacity metrics like available path capacity and tight section capacity in both forward and reverse directions using a single test session, improving network diagnostics.

today: RFC 6802 is published as Informational. It describes a prototype feature developed by Ericsson and tested in real networks, enabling TWAMP-based capacity measurement in both directions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP), defined in RFC 5357, is a standard tool for measuring round-trip delays and loss. Ericsson's Value-Added Octets feature extends TWAMP-Test to measure network capacity metrics such as available path capacity (APC), tight section capacity (TSC), and UDP delivery rate in both the forward and reverse directions.

The extension works by embedding a 10-octet field in the padding of test packets. These octets carry information about packet trains: which packets belong to a train, what the desired reverse transmission rate should be, and the version of the feature being used. The TWAMP reflector (responder) reads these fields, groups packets into trains, buffers them, and sends them back with the specified timing.
sections.plainLanguage: TWAMP is a tool for measuring network performance. This adds extra information to TWAMP packets so you can measure how much traffic a link can handle, in both directions at once.

sections.title: Capacity Measurement Principles
sections.content:
Capacity estimation methods for APC and UDP delivery rate rely on sending and receiving packets in groups called packet trains. Each train is sent at a specific transmission rate, and the goal is to measure how the network path responds. To measure capacity, some trains must be sent faster than the path can handle, creating momentary congestion and allowing the measurement algorithm to infer the available capacity.

At the Session-Sender, trains are constructed with packets separated by a calculated interval. At the Session-Reflector, arriving packets are timestamped. The packet intervals observed at both endpoints, along with packet loss information, allow capacity algorithms to estimate APC, TSC, and delivery rate.
sections.plainLanguage: You send groups of network packets at different speeds and watch how fast they come back. If they slow down, you know the link is full. If they come back at your speed, the link has room.

sections.title: Extended Test Packet Format
sections.content:
The Value-Added Octets feature is embedded at the beginning of the TWAMP-Test packet padding (or after Server Octets if the Reflect Octets mode is used). The 10-octet structure contains: a 4-bit Version field (set to 1 for Version 1), two flag bits (L for Last Seqno in Train and I for Desired Reverse Packet Interval), 10 reserved bits, a 32-bit Last Seqno in Train field (when L=1), and a 32-bit Desired Reverse Packet Interval field (when I=1). If the corresponding flag is not set, those fields are filled with zeros.

The Last Seqno in Train field indicates which packet is expected to be the last in the current train, allowing the reflector to group packets. The Desired Reverse Packet Interval specifies how the reflector should space the reflected packets: zero means as fast as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The 10 extra bytes say: what version this is, which packet is last in this group, and how fast to send the group back.

sections.title: Reflector Behavior
sections.content:
When the Value-Added Octets feature is enabled, the TWAMP Session-Reflector reads the Version field and the L and I flags. If both L and I are set, the reflector buffers packets belonging to the current train (identified by the Last Seqno in Train value) and waits until it has all packets in the train or a timeout occurs. It then transmits the buffered packets back to the sender with the packet interval specified in the Desired Reverse Packet Interval field.

Out-of-order and duplicate packets are handled carefully: they are buffered if the train has not yet been sent, or returned immediately if it has. The reflector must not discard duplicates or reorder packets. If the feature is not recognized or the Version field is unexpected, the reflector falls back to standard TWAMP behavior, returning packets as quickly as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The reflector collects packets from each group, waits for the last one, then sends them back with the spacing the sender asked for.

sections.title: Control Protocol and Deployment
sections.content:
The Value-Added Octets feature is negotiated during TWAMP connection establishment but does not define a new mode bit in the standard Modes field. Instead, bootstrapping the feature is implementation-specific; both the server and controller must be configured or must have agreed to support it. The feature is disabled by default and must only be deployed between hosts managed by the same administrative entity.

The feature works with any TWAMP mode and is designed for backward compatibility. If a controller sends value-added octets to a reflector that does not support them, the reflector treats them as regular padding and returns them as-is, causing the capacity measurement to fail gracefully.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides of the connection agree (outside TWAMP) that they support the new feature, then use it. If the other side does not support it, things still work but the feature just gets ignored.
